claims.title: A shopper session is treated as authority over another shopper's order
claims.description: An authenticated attacker starting as `entity:shopper` can submit a request on `flow:entity:shopper>process:storefront-api>place-order` using another shopper's identifier. `process:storefront-api` does not check each request against caller permissions or verify ownership of the named object, even though this flow carries shopper identifiers and crosses into `boundary:storefront-dmz`. The attacker thereby abuses the broadly effective session access to create or act on orders under another shopper's identity. Second-order, the storefront forwards order contents and shopper identifiers on `flow:process:storefront-api>process:order-service>submit-order`, after which `process:order-service` persists order records containing addresses and card last-four in `store:orders-db`.

quotes.text: Does it check each request against what the caller may do? no; Are permissions narrower than full access, such as roles or scopes? no; Does it check that the caller owns the object it names? no

severity.justification: Likelihood is high because an authenticated `entity:shopper` normally reaches `process:storefront-api` through `flow:entity:shopper>process:storefront-api>place-order`, and the stated per-request permission and ownership checks are absent. Impact is high because the flow carries `pii` and `financial` data and reaches `store:orders-db`, which holds shopper addresses and card last-four and is classified confidential.

mitigations.detail: At `process:storefront-api`, derive the shopper identity from the verified session and reject requests whose order or shopper identifier is not owned by that subject.

mitigations.summary: Apply deny-by-default authorization to storefront operations
mitigations.detail: Use centralized authorization middleware for every route in `process:storefront-api`, with narrowly scoped roles or permissions rather than treating a session cookie as broad order authority.

claims.title: A foothold in the storefront tier can cross into unauthenticated core order processing
claims.description: An attacker who gains control of `process:storefront-api` in `boundary:storefront-dmz` inherits its ability to originate `flow:process:storefront-api>process:order-service>submit-order` across the decided crossing into `boundary:core-services`. That flow has no authentication, and `process:order-service` accepts anything that can reach it. The attacker can therefore escalate from the storefront tier to the core order-processing surface without holding a core-service credential, submitting arbitrary order-capture requests as the storefront. The storefront DMZ placement is an inferred endpoint placement in the derived crossing, but the absent authentication on the crossing flow is stated. Second-order, the reached `process:order-service` reads and writes `store:orders-db`, containing confidential shopper addresses and card last-four, using its application database account.

quotes.text: There is no auth on that gRPC call — the order service accepts anything that can reach it

severity.justification: Likelihood is medium because exploiting the crossing requires a foothold in `process:storefront-api` or its DMZ position, but `flow:process:storefront-api>process:order-service>submit-order` has authentication stated absent. Impact is high because the crossing reaches `process:order-service`, whose downstream `store:orders-db` holds confidential `pii` and `financial` order data.

mitigations.summary: Authenticate and authorize the DMZ-to-core call
mitigations.detail: Require `process:order-service` to authenticate the caller on `flow:process:storefront-api>process:order-service>submit-order` and authorize the propagated shopper or workload identity for each requested operation.

mitigations.summary: Enforce the core boundary at the receiving service
mitigations.detail: Restrict ingress to `process:order-service` to the expected workload identity and network path, while treating any request arriving across the storefront-to-core boundary as untrusted until it passes service-side authorization.

claims.title: The order service's full database account can be abused for arbitrary submitted orders
claims.description: A caller that can reach `process:order-service` can supply order operations that the service does not check against caller permissions, roles, scopes, or object ownership. `process:order-service` then exercises the single application account on `flow:process:order-service>store:orders-db>read-write-orders`, which has full read/write access to `store:orders-db`. This is a confused-deputy authorization failure: the caller does not need the database account, but causes the privileged service to use it on the caller's chosen order and shopper identifiers. Second-order, the resulting authority covers the confidential orders database holding shopper addresses and card last-four, so the caller's scope expands from its own permitted orders to records across the database.

quotes.text: Does it check each request against what the caller may do? no; Are permissions narrower than full access, such as roles or scopes? no; Does it check that the caller owns the object it names? no
a single application account that has full read/write

severity.justification: Likelihood is medium because an attacker must first reach `process:order-service`, which the model describes as internal, but the service's stated authorization checks are absent once reached. Impact is high because the application account has the stated full read/write grant on `store:orders-db`, which is confidential and holds `pii` and `financial` data.

mitigations.summary: Re-authorize the original caller at the order service
mitigations.detail: Propagate a verifiable caller identity over `flow:process:storefront-api>process:order-service>submit-order` and make `process:order-service` enforce operation and object ownership checks before invoking the database account.

mitigations.summary: Narrow database authority by operation and scope
mitigations.detail: Replace the full read/write application account on `flow:process:order-service>store:orders-db>read-write-orders` with narrowly scoped, short-lived privileges and database enforcement that prevents one caller context from operating on another shopper's records.
